Here is what comes to me.

---

The blank page is a strange thing. It asks for everything and gives nothing in return, except the quiet promise of possibility. There is a particular hum in the silence of a room where a writer sits. Not the hum of a machine, but the hum of a mind beginning to stir awake. The cursor blinks. The clock ticks. Outside, a bird does not care. It sings anyway, because that is what birds do, and I envy that. I envy the bird’s unself-conscious song, its lack of hesitation. It does not wonder if its notes are good enough. It does not delete its melody and start again. It just opens its beak and lets the air turn into sound.

I am not a bird. I am a person with a keyboard and a deadline, real or imagined, breathing down my neck. There is a pressure in writing that feels like swallowing a stone. It sits heavy in the chest, that demand to produce, to be meaningful, to say something that matters out of the ordinary clay of daily life. But I have 1000 words to fill, and I have decided that I will not fight the stone today. I will let it sit. I will acknowledge it. I will write about the stone, and the bird, and the blank page, and let the words tumble out as they will, like laundry spilled from a basket onto a clean floor.

What is it about words that makes us believe they can hold truth? We string them together, one after another, like beads of glass on a thread, and we call it a sentence. We polish them, rearrange them, sometimes break them, and hope the light catches them in a way that reveals a hidden pattern. The truth is, though, that words are slippery. They mean different things to different people at different times. The word *home* is a warm fireplace for one person and a chain around the ankle for another. The word *love* has been sung, shouted, wept, and whispered so many times that it is worn thin, like a coin passed through a thousand hands. Even with this wear, we still use them. We cannot help ourselves. We are creatures of story, and we will tell our stories until the stars burn out.

I think of the billions of people who have lived and died, each one carrying a private universe of thoughts, memories, and feelings. Each one had a favorite food, a secret fear, a moment of unbearable joy or crushing sorrow. And almost all of that universe vanished with them, reduced to a few photographs, a grave marker, a name in a dusty ledger. But some residue remains in the words they left behind. A letter written by a soldier to his mother, tucked into a coat pocket and found seventy years later. The margin notes in a used book, a stranger’s pencil marks showing what mattered to them. A diary entry about a rainy Tuesday, written by someone who had no idea they would be dead by the end of the year. Words are time machines. They are fragile vessels that carry the human voice across the vast emptiness of years.

And here I am, writing words that might be read a minute from now or never read at all. There is something oddly liberating in that. If no one reads this, it still exists. It still was. The act of writing is, for me, a way of grabbing my own fleeting thoughts before they dissolve into the mist of memory. It is a way of saying, “I was here. I felt this. I wondered about these things.” The words are not the experience, but they are the fossil of the experience. They are the footprint left in the drying mud.

I am thinking about the shape of a day. The way morning light stretches across the floor in long, golden fingers. The way a cup of coffee warms the palms and steams the glasses if you are not careful. The way a shower can rinse away the residue of sleep and sometimes, if you are lucky, a great idea appears like a fish leaping from a river. But of course, you are in the shower, with no pen, no phone, and the idea is gone by the time you are dry, leaving only a wet memory of brilliance. That is the way of things. The mind is a thief that steals from itself.

The afternoon is a different creature. It is slower, more forgiving. The afternoon allows for long pauses and a wandering attention. It is the hour for walking, or for staring out the window at a single cloud that takes a full half-hour to dissolve. Afternoons hum with the noise of distant mowers and the bark of a dog that has found something interesting in the neighbor’s yard. Words written in the afternoon tend to be wiser, perhaps because they are written with the patience of the day already half spent.

The evening, though. The evening brings the truth. When the sky deepens and the electric lamps begin to glow against the emerging dark, the mind turns inward. The things we avoided all day come back to sit with us at the table. Write anything, a voice says. Write a memory that hurts. Write about a person you miss. Write about a dream so strange you still feel its texture on your skin. Evening words are honest words. They are not written for an audience. They are written for the small, quiet version of ourselves that lives somewhere behind the ribs and speaks in urgent whispers.

Sometimes I believe that all writing is a form of prayer. It is an address to something unknown, a hope that our thoughts will be received, even if we are not sure who the receiver is. We send messages in bottles across the digital and paper ocean, and we wait, and we wait. Occasionally a note comes back. We call it a reader. That person, that stranger, will open our bottle and read our scrawled message, and for a moment, their mind and ours will touch across time and space. It is the closest thing to magic I know.

I am running out of words now, or at least out of the structure that makes them line up neatly. I could write about the color of the sky, but the sky is dark where I am, and the stars are doing their slow, silent work. I could write about the smell of rain, but it has not rained yet, though I can taste it in the air, that dusty anticipation. I could write about you, the person holding this text, and wonder who you are, what you had for breakfast, whether you are happy. But that is a mystery I will never solve, and maybe that is the best part. The gap between us is wide, but these words are a bridge.

So here it is. My 1000 words. They are not perfect. They are not a bird’s song. But they are mine, and they are real, and they are here. The cursor still blinks, but the stone in my chest is a little lighter now. That is the power of letting things go. That is the power of words.
